title: Late cardiovascular drift observable during ultraendurance exercise
authors: Mattsson CM, Stahlberg M, Larsen FJ, Braunschweig F, Ekblom B
population: Eight subjects in 12 h of mixed exercise at controlled intensity and 20 participants in a 53-h adventure race; HR, VO2 and cardiac output measured during fixed-work-rate cycling at 0, 4, 8, 12 h and 0, 20, 53 h
findings: The first step was typical early cardiovascular drift: HR rose while stroke volume and VO2/HR fell, during the first 4-6 h.
A second step, to about 12 h, included reversed HR drift with normalisation of SV and VO2/HR.
When exercise continued to about 50 h, late drift was characterised by increased VO2/HR, decreased peripheral resistance, increased SV and decreased cardiac work.
Cardiac output was maintained throughout; the authors interpret the changes as physiologically appropriate adaptations. VO2 at a fixed work rate was increased at every time point.
limitations: Small samples; mixed-mode exercise and an adventure race, not running; measurements during cycling at fixed work rate; the single-slope picture of drift does not hold, so extrapolation from 1-3 h studies is not supported.
implications: Drift behaviour is not monotonic across ultra durations: do not extrapolate the 1-3 h drift and threshold-decline priors to 100-mile efforts, and do not use HR drift to infer fitness in sessions over about 4 h.
For 100-mile plans, steer long efforts by pace, RPE, fuelling and terrain, and treat drift metrics as descriptive only.
